theme: plate tectonics and sea floor spreading
enonce_markdown: Along the San Andreas Fault in California, two plates slide horizontally past each other. What type of plate boundary is this?

choix.texte: A continental collision boundary with fold mountains

corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Plate boundaries are classified by the relative motion of the plates: moving apart, moving together, or sliding past one another.

### Solution

Plates that slide past each other horizontally, with no crust created and none destroyed, meet at a transform (conservative) boundary. Divergent boundaries create crust, and convergent boundaries destroy it or crumple it.

**Answer: C.**

theme: plate tectonics and sea floor spreading
enonce_markdown: Radiometric dating of basalt samples taken across the floor of the Atlantic Ocean shows that the age of the oceanic crust changes with the position of the sample. Where is the youngest crust found?

choix.texte: At the crest of the mid-ocean ridge, where new crust is forming
Beside the deep-sea trenches on the ocean margins
On the continental shelf next to the coast
Everywhere, because the ocean floor formed in a single event

corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

In sea floor spreading, new lithosphere is made at the ridge axis and carried away on both sides, so age increases with distance from the ridge.

### Solution

Magma rises and solidifies at the ridge crest, so the rock there is newest. The crust moves away from the ridge and gets older with distance. The oldest oceanic crust (about 180 million years) lies far from the ridge, and it is destroyed in subduction zones.

**Answer: A.**

theme: plate tectonics and sea floor spreading
enonce_markdown: Basalt on the sea floor 1000 km from the axis of a mid-ocean ridge is dated at 40 million years. Assuming a constant rate, what is the average speed at which this crust has moved away from the ridge axis?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Speed $=\dfrac{\text{distance}}{\text{time}}$. Convert both to the same units: $1\ \mathrm{km} = 10^{5}\ \mathrm{cm}$.

### Solution

Distance: $1000\ \mathrm{km} = 1.0 \times 10^{8}\ \mathrm{cm}$. Time: $40 \times 10^{6}$ years.

Speed $= \dfrac{1.0 \times 10^{8}}{4.0 \times 10^{7}} = 2.5\ \mathrm{cm\,yr^{-1}}$.

The value $25$ is obtained by leaving the result in km per million years ($1000/40 = 25\ \mathrm{km\,Ma^{-1}}$) and forgetting that $1\ \mathrm{km\,Ma^{-1}} = 0.1\ \mathrm{cm\,yr^{-1}}$.

**Answer: B.**

theme: plate tectonics and sea floor spreading
enonce_markdown: Dense oceanic lithosphere is subducted beneath continental lithosphere along the western margin of a continent. Which pair of features is formed?

choix.texte: A mid-ocean ridge on the ocean side and a rift valley on the continent
A trench on the ocean side and a chain of basaltic shield volcanoes at the trench
A transform fault on the ocean side and a continental rift with granite intrusions
A deep-sea trench on the ocean side and a chain of andesitic volcanoes on the continent

corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

At an ocean-continent convergent boundary the denser oceanic plate bends downwards (trench) and the water released from the slab triggers melting in the mantle wedge above it.

### Solution

The subducting slab forms a deep-sea trench at the surface. At about 100 km depth, water driven from the slab lowers the melting point of the mantle wedge, and the magma rises, mixes with continental crust and erupts as intermediate (andesitic) volcanoes, as in the Andes. Ridges and rifts are features of divergent boundaries.

**Answer: D.**

theme: plate tectonics and sea floor spreading
enonce_markdown: Explain how the pattern of magnetic stripes on the ocean floor provides evidence for sea floor spreading.
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Hot basalt records the direction of the Earth's magnetic field at the moment it cools below its Curie temperature, and the field has reversed many times.

### Solution

**Recording.** Basalt erupted at the ridge contains magnetic minerals (magnetite) that line up with the Earth's magnetic field as the lava cools, and keep this direction. Rock formed during normal polarity gives a stronger-than-average reading on a magnetometer (positive anomaly), and rock formed during reversed polarity gives a weaker one (negative anomaly).

**Stripes.** The Earth's field has reversed polarity many times. As new crust forms at the ridge and moves away on either side, it forms parallel stripes of alternating polarity.

**Symmetry.** The stripes form a mirror image on both sides of the ridge, and their widths match across the ridge. This is exactly what is predicted if the crust is created at the axis and split symmetrically (Vine and Matthews, 1963).

**Dating.** The sequence of stripes matches the dated record of reversals on land, which gives an age to each stripe. The age increases with distance from the ridge, which confirms the rate of spreading.

A static ocean floor would not produce symmetrical stripes that match the time scale of reversals.

theme: plate tectonics and sea floor spreading
enonce_markdown: A volcanic island chain lies on a plate moving over a stationary mantle hot spot. The active volcano is at the south-east end. An extinct island 350 km to the north-west of the active volcano has a radiometric age of 4.2 million years. What is the average speed of the plate over the hot spot?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

If the hot spot is fixed, the distance between an extinct volcano and the active one, divided by the age of the extinct volcano, is the speed of the plate. Keep track of the units: $1\ \mathrm{km\,Ma^{-1}} = 0.1\ \mathrm{cm\,yr^{-1}}$.

### Solution

Speed $= \dfrac{350\ \mathrm{km}}{4.2\ \mathrm{Ma}} = 83.3\ \mathrm{km\,Ma^{-1}}$.

In centimetres per year: $\dfrac{350 \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{cm}}{4.2 \times 10^{6}\ \mathrm{yr}} = 8.3\ \mathrm{cm\,yr^{-1}}$.

The plate therefore moves towards the north-west at about 8 cm per year, a speed typical of a fast plate. The values 83 and 830 come from unit conversion slips.

**Answer: A.**
